description: We’re Team Lagrange Point, six builders from Iligan City, Philippines. Our team combines front-end and UI/UX design, lunar science research, data analysis, AI and back-end engineering, and media and animation. Together we built Gnomon to make NASA’s lunar data readable at a glance, so anyone can see where the Moon stays lit up.
summary:
What We Developed

Gnomon is a web app that helps determine whether a lunar landing site is suitable for a mission. Users can select a location near the Moon's south pole, choose a landing date, and set the mission duration. Within seconds, Gnomon provides a GO, RISKY, or NO-GO verdict based on two essential factors: sunlight for solar power and Earth visibility for communication.

It shows when the Sun and Earth are visible, how long they disappear behind lunar terrain, and whether a lander's battery can survive periods without sunlight. Users can compare landing sites, find the best landing dates, explore the Moon in 3D, and simulate Earth-Moon orbits. An AI guide named Five also answers questions through chat and voice.

How It Addresses the Challenge

Gnomon uses NASA data, including JPL Horizons and LRO LOLA terrain data, to calculate solar and Earth visibility. We also validated our calculations against independent NASA datasets to ensure accuracy.

Why It Matters

With Artemis and future missions targeting the lunar south pole, choosing the right landing site is critical. Even a small ridge can block sunlight or communication. Gnomon makes these risks visible before landing, helping mission planners decide where to land, when to operate, and how long a lander can safely stay.
details:
What it does and how it works

Gnomon is a free browser app that tells you in seconds whether a lunar landing site and date will work. You pick a site, a landing date and a mission length, and Gnomon gives a GO, RISKY or NO-GO verdict. The verdict is based on sunlight for power and Earth in view for direct contact.

It works in three steps:

  1. NASA JPL Horizons gives the Sun’s and Earth’s direction and height in the sky at each of 9 sites, every 2 hours, from November 2026 to December 2028.
  2. NASA LRO LOLA terrain from Goddard’s PGDA (5 m maps where available, 20 m and 240 m polar mosaics) gives each site a 360° skyline, including the Moon’s curvature.
  3. Gnomon counts the hours the Sun and Earth are above that skyline during the mission, and finds the longest blackout.

The app includes:

  • A Slip Test that shows what a 1 to 14 day launch delay does to the verdict.
  • A Calendar that colors every landing day GO, RISKY or NO-GO.
  • Compare, which ranks all sites for the same dates.
  • A Power check that tests a lander’s battery against the dark periods.
  • A Landing area view of the verdict around the touchdown point.
  • 3D views: a NASA-textured globe, true-scale terrain with a shadow timelapse, and an Earth–Moon orbit view.
  • Shareable links and a printable report.
  • Five, an AI guide that answers questions about Gnomon and its sites by text or voice. It only answers from the app’s own information.

Benefits and intended impact

Today, checking one site means pulling Sun and Earth positions from Horizons one site at a time, viewing terrain in Moon Trek and QuickMap, and cross-checking dates by hand. A launch slip means starting over. Gnomon puts all of it on one screen. At the south pole, where Artemis and other missions are going, the Sun barely clears the horizon, so one ridge or a few days’ delay can decide whether a lander survives. Gnomon makes that risk visible early, for mission planners, students and the public.

How we checked it

  • Our Sun and Earth positions match an independent calculation from JPL’s DE421 ephemeris within 0.0005°, across 170,874 positions.
  • Our sunlight figures are within 2.1 points on average of NASA’s PGDA polar illumination maps. At 7 of 7 polar sites, our value falls inside NASA’s own range within 500 m.

Tools and languages

  • Front end: TypeScript and React, built with Vite and Tailwind CSS. The 3D views use three.js through React Three Fiber and drei, with Framer Motion for animation and Recharts for charts.
  • Data pipeline: Python with NumPy, rasterio and pyproj. Validation used jplephem and SpiceyPy.
  • Five: Google Gemini API for answers and voice input, and ElevenLabs for Five’s spoken replies.
  • Hosting: Vercel, with the custom domain served through Cloudflare.
  • Hardware: our own laptops and PCs. No special hardware.

What makes it creative

It turns heavy ephemeris and terrain data into one plain verdict you can understand at a glance. You can drag the landing date and watch the verdict change. And you can see the skyline, shadows, Sun and Earth move on real NASA terrain.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy, checked against NASA’s own results.
  • Honesty: the verdict is a screening tool using our own thresholds, not NASA criteria, and the app says so.
  • Launch delays, since real missions slip.
  • Both power and communications needs.
  • Running on phones, tablets and laptops.
  • Accessibility, and plain language for non-experts.
